### Why this matters
At work you open a solution someone else created. Interviews and side projects expect you to start from nothing: pick a folder layout, split the code into layers and explain why the arrows point the way they do. Every later week builds on today, so understand each command instead of copying it.

### What you'll build
- A Git repo `jobhunt/` with `/api` for .NET (the React part creates `/web` today)
- A solution `JobHunt` in `/api` (in .NET 10, `dotnet new sln` creates the `.slnx` format)
- Four projects under `api/src/`: `JobHunt.Domain`, `JobHunt.Application`, `JobHunt.Infrastructure` (class libraries) and `JobHunt.Api` (empty web project)
- References: Api → Application → Domain, Infrastructure → Application, Api → Infrastructure (only so `Program.cs` can register it later)

### Step by step
1. Run `dotnet --version` (you need 10.x), then `git init` in `jobhunt/` and create a branch `feature/skeleton`.
2. Inside `api`, run `dotnet new sln -n JobHunt` and open the `.slnx` file. It is plain XML.
3. Create the libraries with `dotnet new classlib -n JobHunt.Domain -o src/JobHunt.Domain`, then Application and Infrastructure. Delete `Class1.cs`.
4. Create the API with `dotnet new web -n JobHunt.Api -o src/JobHunt.Api`.
5. Add each project with `dotnet sln add`, then wire the references with `dotnet add <project> reference <project>`.
6. Run `dotnet build` and commit.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `dotnet build` passes from `/api`
- [ ] `dotnet sln list` shows exactly four projects
- [ ] Domain references nothing; Application references only Domain
- [ ] Work is on `feature/skeleton`, not `main`

### Hints
- `dotnet list <project> reference` prints a project's references so you can check the arrows.
- Draw the four boxes on paper first. Arrows point inward, toward Domain.

### Common mistakes
- Running `dotnet new` inside another project folder and ending up with nested projects.
- Referencing Infrastructure from Application "just for now". The inner layer then knows the database.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a `Directory.Build.props` that sets `Nullable` and `ImplicitUsings` once for every project.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between a solution and a project, and what does each compile into?
- Why does only the Api project get to reference Infrastructure?
- What would break if Domain referenced Application?

### Why this matters
At work someone else chose the build tool, the lint rules and the TypeScript settings. Knowing what Vite does and what `strict` turns on is what separates "I can edit components" from "I can start a front end".

### What you'll build
- `/web`: a Vite app from the `react-ts` template (React 19 + TypeScript)
- `strict: true` confirmed, plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`
- ESLint (already in the template) and Prettier, with `lint` and `format` npm scripts
- The template's demo counter and logos removed

### Step by step
1. Check `node --version`. Use a current LTS release (22 or later).
2. From the repo root run `npm create vite@latest web -- --template react-ts`, then `cd web` and `npm install`.
3. Run `npm run dev` and open the URL. Then read `package.json`, `vite.config.ts`, `tsconfig.app.json` and `eslint.config.js` and write one line in your notes about what each does.
4. In `tsconfig.app.json` confirm `strict` is `true` and add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
5. Install `prettier` and `eslint-config-prettier` as dev dependencies, add a `.prettierrc`, and add the Prettier config last in the ESLint config.
6. Add `"format": "prettier --write ."` to the scripts.
7. Replace `App.tsx` with a single heading, delete the demo assets, run `npm run lint` and `npm run build`, and commit.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `npm run build` runs `tsc` and Vite with zero errors
- [ ] `npm run lint` passes with zero warnings
- [ ] `strict` and `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` are on
- [ ] Demo counter and logos are gone

### Hints
- Look at the `build` script: it type-checks first and only then bundles.
- Set your editor to format on save with Prettier once, now.

### Common mistakes
- Turning off `strict` later to make an error go away. Fix the type instead.
- Running ESLint style rules and Prettier together, so they fight forever. `eslint-config-prettier` turns the clashing rules off.
- Creating the app inside `/api` by accident. It lives next to it.

### Check your understanding
- What does Vite do in dev that it does not do in a production build?
- Name three checks that `strict` turns on.
- Why does `build` run `tsc` before Vite?

### Why this matters
A health endpoint is the first thing load balancers, containers and your own front end call. Building it by hand makes you read `Program.cs` line by line: the builder, the services, the app and the pipeline. "Walk me through Program.cs" is a common .NET interview question.

### What you'll build
- `GET /health` in `JobHunt.Api` returning `{ "status": "Healthy", "version": "1.0.0", "environment": "Development" }`
- A `HealthResponse` positional record for the shape
- The endpoint in its own extension method `MapHealthEndpoints()`, so `Program.cs` stays short

### Step by step
1. Open `Program.cs` and label each part with a comment: builder, service registration, `Build()`, middleware pipeline, endpoints, `Run()`.
2. Create `HealthResponse(string Status, string Version, string Environment)`.
3. Write a static class with an extension method on `IEndpointRouteBuilder` that calls `MapGet("/health", ...)` and returns `TypedResults.Ok(...)`.
4. Inject `IHostEnvironment` as a handler parameter and use its `EnvironmentName`. Hard-code the version for now; Wednesday moves it to configuration.
5. Run with `dotnet run` and call the endpoint from the browser or a `.http` file.

```csharp
public static IEndpointRouteBuilder MapHealthEndpoints(this IEndpointRouteBuilder app)
{
    app.MapGet("/health", (IHostEnvironment env) => /* TODO */);
    return app;
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `GET /health` returns 200 with `application/json`
- [ ] Property names are camelCase
- [ ] The environment comes from `IHostEnvironment`, not a string literal
- [ ] `Program.cs` has no inline handler

### Hints
- Handlers can take services as parameters; the framework resolves them from DI.
- `TypedResults.Ok(...)` makes the status code explicit and shows up in OpenAPI metadata later.

### Common mistakes
- Using the full `webapi` template sample code instead of writing the handler.
- Confusing this with the built-in `AddHealthChecks`. It exists; today the goal is to write a handler yourself.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between `WebApplicationBuilder` and `WebApplication`?
- Where does a minimal API handler get its parameters from?
- What does middleware order mean, and where do endpoints sit in it?

### Why this matters
Strict TypeScript catches the bugs interviewers love to ask about: `undefined is not a function`, a typo in a status string, a missing field. Today you describe the JSON your .NET part returns as a type, so the compiler checks every place you use it.

### What you'll build
- `web/src/types/health.ts` with a `HealthStatus` interface: `status`, `version`, `environment`
- `status` typed as a union, for example `"Healthy" | "Degraded" | "Unhealthy"`, not `string`
- A `HealthCard` component with typed props that renders a sample `HealthStatus`
- A colour or label chosen with a `switch` on `status`

The shape matches the `/health` JSON from today's .NET part.

### Step by step
1. Write the `HealthStatus` interface and a `HealthState` union type.
2. Create `const sample: HealthStatus = { ... }` and try leaving out a field or misspelling `"Healthy"` to read the errors.
3. Write `HealthCard({ health }: HealthCardProps)` as a plain function with a props interface.
4. Add a function `labelFor(status: HealthState): string` with a `switch` and assign the value to `never` in the `default` case.
5. Render `<HealthCard health={sample} />` from `App.tsx`, run `npm run build`.

```ts
type HealthState = "Healthy" | "Degraded" | "Unhealthy";
export interface HealthStatus { status: HealthState; /* TODO */ }
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No `any` anywhere
- [ ] `status` is a union of literals
- [ ] Adding a new union member makes `labelFor` fail to compile until handled
- [ ] `npm run build` passes

### Hints
- Use `interface` for object shapes and props, `type` for unions. Be ready to explain the difference.
- Optional fields (`version?: string`) force you to handle `undefined` under strict null checks.

### Common mistakes
- Using `React.FC` by habit. Plain functions with typed props are the current recommendation.
- Typing `status` as `string`, which accepts any typo.

### Check your understanding
- When would you choose a union of literals over a TypeScript `enum`?
- What does strict null checking change about `user.name.length`?
- How does the `never` trick make a `switch` exhaustive?
1-2-api:
### Why this matters
Every real deployment runs the same build with different settings. Knowing which configuration source wins, and how the environment name is chosen, saves hours of "works on my machine" debugging and is a standard interview question.

### What you'll build
- An `App` section in `appsettings.json` with `Version` and `DisplayName`
- An override of `DisplayName` in `appsettings.Development.json`
- A second launch profile in `launchSettings.json` with `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` set to `Production`
- `/health` reading `App:Version` from `IConfiguration` and returning `displayName` as an extra field

### Step by step
1. Add the `App` section to `appsettings.json` and only `DisplayName` to the Development file.
2. Inject `IConfiguration` into the handler and read `config["App:Version"]`.
3. Open `Properties/launchSettings.json`, copy the existing profile and set its environment to `Production`.
4. Run with `dotnet run --launch-profile <name>` for each profile and compare the JSON.
5. Override the version from the shell with an environment variable named `App__Version` and see that it wins.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No hard-coded version in C#
- [ ] Development and Production return different `environment` and `displayName`
- [ ] An `App__Version` environment variable overrides the file value
- [ ] No secrets in `appsettings.json`

### Hints
- Sources are layered: `appsettings.json`, then `appsettings.{Environment}.json`, then user secrets (Development only), environment variables, command line. Later wins.
- The double underscore in environment variable names maps to the `:` separator.

### Common mistakes
- Putting real secrets into `appsettings.json`. It is committed; secrets come later.
- Thinking `launchSettings.json` is used in production. It is only read by `dotnet run` and IDEs on your machine.

### Stretch (optional)
- Read the version from the assembly instead and keep configuration only for the display name.

### Check your understanding
- In which order are the configuration sources applied, and which wins?
- Where does the environment name come from when you deploy?
- Why is `launchSettings.json` not a deployment setting?

### Why this matters
Fetching in an effect with proper loading and error handling is the base you will replace with TanStack Query in week 5, so you will know exactly what it saves you. Today the React part calls the `/health` endpoint from the .NET part.

### What you'll build
- `getHealth(signal?)` that calls `/health` with `fetch` and returns `Promise<HealthStatus>`
- A single `API_BASE_URL` constant (week 3 replaces it)
- A `HealthBadge` component with three states: loading, ok and error

### Step by step
1. Write `getHealth`: call `fetch`, throw when `!res.ok`, return the parsed JSON as `HealthStatus`.
2. In `HealthBadge`, keep `data`, `error` and `loading` in `useState`.
3. In `useEffect`, define an async function inside and call it. Give the effect an explicit `[]` dependency array.
4. Add a cleanup that ignores a late result (an `ignore` flag or an `AbortController`).
5. Run both apps. The call is probably blocked: read the console error and the Network tab. That is your error state working; Thursday's .NET part adds CORS and the badge turns green.
6. Stop the API and reload to see a network failure end in the same error state.

```ts
export async function getHealth(signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<HealthStatus> {
  const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}/health`, { signal });
  // TODO: check res.ok, parse and return
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Loading, ok and error states are all visible at some point
- [ ] Network failures and non-2xx responses both end in the error state
- [ ] The effect has a cleanup and a dependency array
- [ ] No `any` in the fetch code

### Hints
- `fetch` only rejects on network failure. A 500 still resolves, so check `res.ok`.
- In development, StrictMode runs effects twice on mount. That is why the cleanup matters.

### Common mistakes
- Making the effect callback itself `async`. It must return nothing or a cleanup function.
- Treating `res.json()` as typed. It returns `any`; the annotation is a promise you make, not a check.

### Check your understanding
- Why does `fetch` resolve for a 500 response?
- Why does the effect run twice in development, and why is that useful?
- What would go wrong without the cleanup if the component unmounted mid-request?
1-3-api:
### Why this matters
Yesterday the browser blocked your React app. Many developers paste `AllowAnyOrigin` and move on. You will understand why the browser blocks the call, what a preflight is, and how to allow exactly one origin. This unblocks the badge from Wednesday's React part.

### What you'll build
- A `Cors:AllowedOrigins` array in `appsettings.Development.json` with the Vite dev origin (for example `http://localhost:5173`)
- A named CORS policy registered with `AddCors` that reads those origins
- `UseCors("<name>")` in the pipeline before the endpoints

### Step by step
1. Read the blocked request in the browser's Network tab once more and write down which header was missing.
2. Add the origins array to the Development settings file.
3. Bind it with `builder.Configuration.GetSection(...).Get<string[]>()` and call `AddCors(o => o.AddPolicy(name, p => p.WithOrigins(origins)...))`.
4. Add `app.UseCors(name)` before you map the endpoints.
5. Reload the web app and find `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` in the response headers.
6. Change the configured port to a wrong one and confirm the badge breaks again.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No `AllowAnyOrigin` anywhere
- [ ] Origins come from configuration, not a C# literal
- [ ] The badge shows ok with the API running
- [ ] A wrong origin in config breaks the call again

### Hints
- CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. The server only says which origins it trusts. That is why a `.http` file call worked without CORS.
- Origin means scheme + host + port. `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173` are different origins.
- A simple `GET` has no preflight; a `PUT` with JSON will send an `OPTIONS` request first.

### Common mistakes
- Calling `UseCors` after the endpoints, so headers never appear.
- A trailing slash in the origin string, which never matches.
- Thinking CORS protects your API from scripts or curl. It does not; it protects users' browsers.

### Check your understanding
- What makes two URLs the "same origin"?
- When does the browser send a preflight `OPTIONS` request?
- Why can Postman call the API when the browser cannot?

### Why this matters
Building from scratch means you will break things often. A fast loop (save, see the change) and the habit of using a debugger and logs instead of guessing are what make you quick. Interviewers notice when you can set a breakpoint and read a stack instead of adding print lines.

### What you'll build
- The API running under `dotnet watch` with hot reload
- A breakpoint hit inside the `/health` handler in your editor's debugger
- An `ILogger` log line in the handler at Information level
- A log level override in `appsettings.Development.json` so your namespace logs at Debug

### Step by step
1. Run `dotnet watch --project src/JobHunt.Api` and change the status string. Watch the console say it applied the change.
2. Stop it. Start the API from your editor's debugger (VS Code with the C# Dev Kit, Visual Studio or Rider), set a breakpoint in the handler and call `/health`.
3. At the breakpoint, inspect `env`, step over a line and look at the call stack.
4. Inject `ILogger<Program>` (or a logger for your endpoint class) and log the environment with a message template: `"Health checked in {Environment}"`.
5. Add a `Logging:LogLevel` entry for `JobHunt` at `Debug` and add one `LogDebug` line to prove it appears.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Hot reload applied at least one change without a restart
- [ ] A breakpoint in the handler was hit
- [ ] Log lines use message templates, not string interpolation
- [ ] The Debug line shows only in Development

### Hints
- Some edits (for example changing a record's shape) are "rude edits" that need a restart; `dotnet watch` will offer it.
- Message templates keep `Environment` as a structured property that log tools can search.

### Common mistakes
- Using `$"..."` in log calls, which loses the structure and allocates even when the level is off.
- Leaving `Console.WriteLine` debugging in committed code.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between hot reload and a restart?
- Why are message templates better than interpolated strings in logs?
- How do log level overrides by category work?

### Why this matters
A project that needs five terminal tabs and a secret ritual to start is a project nobody wants to run. One command, a clean `.gitignore` and a clear README are what reviewers notice first in a take-home or portfolio repo. Today you also finish the week: the PR "Skeleton".

### What you'll build
- A root `package.json` (`"private": true`) with a process runner such as `concurrently` and scripts `dev:api`, `dev:web`, `dev`, `build`
- A root `.gitignore` for .NET (`bin/`, `obj/`, `.vs/`) and Node (`node_modules/`, `dist/`, `.env.local`)
- README sections: prerequisites, first run, scripts, folder layout
- React DevTools installed in your browser

### Step by step
1. In the root run `npm init -y`, set `"private": true`, install `concurrently` as a dev dependency.
2. Add `dev:api` (`dotnet watch --project api/src/JobHunt.Api`), `dev:web` (`npm --prefix web run dev`) and a `dev` script that runs both with name prefixes.
3. Add `build` that builds the solution and the web app and stops on the first failure.
4. Create `.gitignore` (`dotnet new gitignore` is a good base, then add the Node entries). Check `git status` shows no `bin`, `obj` or `node_modules`.
5. Install React DevTools, open the Components tab and find `HealthBadge` and its state.
6. Write the README, clone the repo into a temp folder and follow it exactly.
7. Push and open the PR "Skeleton". Read the whole diff once before merging.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `npm run dev` starts both apps with prefixed output
- [ ] `npm run build` fails if either app fails
- [ ] `git status` is clean after a build
- [ ] A fresh clone works using only the README
- [ ] PR "Skeleton" is merged into `main`

### Hints
- npm scripts have `node_modules/.bin` on the path, so local tools run without `npx`.
- If something ignored was already committed, `git rm -r --cached <path>` removes it from the index only.

### Common mistakes
- Using `&` between commands in a script: it behaves differently on Windows and Linux.
- Commit messages like "fix" or "wip". Use the imperative: "Add health endpoint".

### Check your understanding
- Why put scripts in a root `package.json` instead of a shell script?
- What does `git rm --cached` do that plain `git rm` does not?
- What can React DevTools show you that the Elements tab cannot?
1-4-checkpoint:
### The drill
From a blank folder, build a minimal API with one JSON endpoint and a Vite React page that fetches and shows that JSON, in 25 minutes.

### Rules
- Work in a new empty folder outside the JobHunt repo.
- Create everything with the CLI: `dotnet new` and `npm create vite`.
- Official docs are allowed, but try without them first and note every lookup. No AI assistants, no copying from JobHunt.
- Set a 25 minute timer and stop when it rings, finished or not.

### Must include
- An empty web project with one endpoint, for example `GET /quote` returning a record like `{ "text": "...", "author": "..." }`
- A CORS policy that allows only the Vite dev origin
- A strict TypeScript type for the response, with no `any`
- `fetch` inside `useEffect` with loading and error states and a cleanup
- Both apps running at the same time and the page showing the JSON

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished within 25 minutes
- [ ] Wrote the `dotnet new` and `npm create vite` commands without looking them up
- [ ] CORS allows one origin, not any origin
- [ ] The fetch checks `response.ok`
- [ ] The effect has a cleanup and a dependency array
- [ ] You can explain why the browser blocked the call before CORS was added
- [ ] Your lookup list has three items or fewer

### If you got stuck
- CLI commands, solutions and projects: Monday, .NET part.
- Vite setup and strict mode: Monday, React part.
- `MapGet`, records as responses, `Program.cs` order: Tuesday, .NET part.
- Types and unions for the response: Tuesday, React part.
- `fetch`, `useEffect` and cleanup: Wednesday, React part.
- CORS: Thursday, .NET part.
2-0-api:
### Why this matters
The domain model is the vocabulary of the whole app: every table, endpoint and screen starts here. Choosing between class, record and struct is a classic C# interview topic, and nullable reference types catch null bugs at compile time.

### What you'll build
In `JobHunt.Domain`, on a branch `feature/domain-model`:
- `ApplicationStatus` enum: `Applied`, `Interviewing`, `Offer`, `Rejected`
- `Company` class: `Id` (`Guid`), `Name` (required), `Website?`, `Location?`
- `JobApplication` class: `Id`, `CompanyId` and a `Company` reference, `RoleTitle`, `AppliedOn` (`DateOnly`), `Status`, `SourceUrl?` and a read-only `Interviews` collection
- `Interview` class: `Id`, `JobApplicationId`, `Round`, `ScheduledAt` (`DateTimeOffset`), `Notes?`

### Step by step
1. Create folders `Companies`, `Applications` and `Common`.
2. Write the enum first and decide the starting status for a new application.
3. Write the entities as classes with `private set` properties and constructors taking every required value. Take a `Company` and set both `Company` and `CompanyId`. Ids: `Guid.CreateVersion7()`.
4. Back `Interviews` with a private `List<Interview>` exposed as `IReadOnlyCollection<Interview>`.
5. Mark only truly optional values with `?` and guard required strings in constructors.
6. Run `dotnet build -warnaserror` and fix every nullable warning properly.

```csharp
public sealed class JobApplication
{
    private readonly List<Interview> _interviews = [];
    public Guid Id { get; private set; }
    public IReadOnlyCollection<Interview> Interviews => _interviews;
    // TODO: constructor with guards, other properties
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Zero warnings with `-warnaserror`
- [ ] No public setters, and `Interviews` is read-only from outside
- [ ] Domain has no references
- [ ] Names match exactly

### Hints
- `ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(value)` is a one-line guard.
- `DateOnly` fits "applied on"; `DateTimeOffset` fits "interview at 10:00 in a time zone".

### Common mistakes
- Making entities records: two applications with the same data would compare equal.
- Silencing warnings with `null!`.

### Check your understanding
- What does the compiler generate for a `record` that it does not for a `class`?
- When would you pick a `record struct`?
- Nullable reference types are compile-time only. What does that mean for incoming JSON?
2-0-web:
### Why this matters
The front end needs its own model of the domain. Mirroring C# types in TypeScript, and knowing where they differ (dates arrive as strings, enums as text), prevents a whole class of runtime bugs. Today's .NET part writes the C# side of the same model.

### What you'll build
In `web/src/types/application.ts`:
- `ApplicationStatus` as a union of string literals: `"Applied" | "Interviewing" | "Offer" | "Rejected"`
- `Company`, `JobApplication` and `Interview` types mirroring the C# entities
- Dates typed as `string` (ISO format), because that is what JSON gives you
- An exported `applicationStatuses` array so the UI can loop over every status

### Step by step
1. Open your C# classes side by side and write each TypeScript type field by field.
2. Decide how optional fields look: `website?: string` (may be missing) or `website: string | null` (always present, maybe null). The API will send `null`, so prefer the second.
3. Decide how an application shows its company name: embed `company: { id; name }` or keep only `companyId`. Pick one and note why.
4. Write `const applicationStatuses = [...] as const` and derive the union from it with `(typeof applicationStatuses)[number]`.
5. Create a `sample` object typed as `JobApplication` in a scratch file and run `npm run build`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No `any`
- [ ] The status union has exactly the four C# values, spelled the same
- [ ] Dates are `string`, not `Date`
- [ ] Optional C# fields are `T | null` in TypeScript

### Hints
- `type` and `interface` both work for object shapes. Pick one convention for models and stay consistent.
- `as const` keeps literal types instead of widening them to `string`.

### Common mistakes
- Typing dates as `Date`. JSON has no date type; you get strings until you convert them.
- Using a TypeScript `enum` by habit. Unions of strings match JSON exactly and add no runtime code.
- Different casing from the API. JSON from ASP.NET Core is camelCase by default.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a `Paged<T>` generic type now; you will need it in week 5.

### Check your understanding
- Why are dates `string` in your TypeScript types?
- What is the difference between `field?: T` and `field: T | null`?
- How does `as const` let you get a union and an array from one source?
2-1-api:
### Why this matters
If any code can write `application.Status = Offer`, the rules live in whoever remembers them. Putting rules inside the entity means the API, a background job and a test all go through the same check. "Where do your business rules live?" is a favourite design question.

### What you'll build
- Allowed transitions: `Applied` → `Interviewing` or `Rejected`; `Interviewing` → `Offer` or `Rejected`; `Offer` and `Rejected` are final
- Methods on `JobApplication`: `StartInterviewing()`, `ReceiveOffer()`, `Reject()`
- An abstract `DomainException` in `Common` and `InvalidStatusTransitionException` carrying `From` and `To`

### Why this matters
Every real list is paged. Doing it badly gives duplicates or missing rows between pages and slow counts. Offset vs keyset paging is a classic database interview question: you will build one and explain the other.

### Why this matters
Filters and sorts are only fast when the database can find rows without reading the whole table. Choosing an index from your real queries, and proving it with a plan, is what separates "I added an index" from "I fixed the slow query". Interviewers love the follow-up: "what does an index cost?"

### What you'll build
- About 2,000 extra seed rows in a Development-only script so plans are meaningful

2. Copy the SQL for a typical request (status filter, default sort, page 1) from the log.
3. Run it in SSMS or Azure Data Studio with the actual plan on. Note scans and the estimated cost.
4. Add the indexes in configuration and run `migrations add AddListIndexes`. Read the generated SQL.

- Indexing every column "just in case": each index slows writes and takes space.

Auth code fails quietly: a default you never looked at can let an expired token live five extra minutes. ### Why this matters
Two tabs, one application. Tab A moves it to `Offer`, tab B, still showing `Interviewing`, rejects it. Without concurrency control the last write silently wins: the lost update. Optimistic concurrency detects it without locks: an update succeeds only if the row's version has not changed, and the loser gets 409. Today's React part sends this version with every move.

### What you'll build
- A `RowVersion` shadow property with `IsRowVersion()` (Domain stays persistence-free) and a migration
- `Version` (base64) in the list and detail DTOs, read in projections with `EF.Property<byte[]>(...)`
- `Version` required in `ChangeStatusRequest` and `UpdateApplicationRequest`
- A repository method that sets the property's original value to the client's version
- `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` translated in Infrastructure into an Application `ConcurrencyConflictException`, mapped to 409

### Step by step
1. Read the EF page: concurrency token vs `rowversion`.
2. Configure the shadow property, add the migration, check the column type.
3. Project the version into DTOs as base64.
4. In commands: load, set the expected version, call the domain, save.
5. Catch the EF exception where `SaveChangesAsync` lives and throw your own.
6. Map it to 409 next to yesterday's 422.
7. GET one application, copy its version, send two PATCHes with it.

```csharp
builder.Property<byte[]>("RowVersion").IsRowVersion();
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A stale version returns 409, never a silent overwrite
- [ ] Domain has no `byte[]` or EF attributes
- [ ] Application never sees `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`
- [ ] A missing version returns 400

### Hints
- Setting the original value puts the client's version in the `UPDATE ... WHERE`.
- The week 6 edit form breaks today until it sends `version`; today's React part fixes it.
- HTTP's own version of this is `ETag` with `If-Match` and 412.

### Common mistakes
- Comparing versions by hand, leaving a race between load and save.
- Retrying a 409 automatically: last write wins with extra steps.

### Check your understanding
- What is a lost update?
- How does `rowversion` prevent it without locking?
- Why 409 here and not 422?

### Why this matters
A client that writes and does not get the new version back can only write once: its next request is stale by definition. Returning the new state and version after every change lets the client update its cache without another GET. Today's React part writes this response straight into the cache.

### What you'll build
- `ChangeStatusAsync` and `UpdateAsync` returning the updated `ApplicationDto` including the new version
- The new `RowVersion` read after `SaveChangesAsync` (EF refreshes store-generated values on tracked entities)
- Endpoints returning `TypedResults.Ok(dto)`
- A `.http` sequence: GET, PATCH with that version, PATCH with the returned version, PATCH with the first version again

### Step by step
1. After saving, read the shadow property's current value through the change tracker in Infrastructure.
2. Decide how to build the DTO: map the tracked entity, or re-query through `IApplicationQueries`. Write one line on the trade-off.
3. Return the DTO from both write endpoints.
4. Run the sequence and check: the second PATCH succeeds, the third gets 409.
5. Make sure the version string format matches what the list and detail queries return.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every successful write returns the new version
- [ ] Chained writes with returned versions all succeed
- [ ] The returned DTO matches what a GET returns
- [ ] Application code still knows nothing about `byte[]` row versions beyond a string

### Hints
- EF reads `rowversion` back in the same round trip as the `UPDATE`, so no extra query is needed if you use the tracked entity.
- A re-query is simpler to keep identical to GET but costs one more round trip. Either is fine if you can defend it.

### Common mistakes
- Returning 204 from writes, so the client must GET before it can write again.
- Encoding the version differently in write responses and reads.

### Stretch (optional)
- Also return the version as an `ETag` header.

### Check your understanding
- Why must writes return the new version?
- Where does EF get the new `rowversion` value from?
- What does a client do with the response instead of refetching?

### Why this matters
Shared data makes tests flaky: one test's leftovers change another's counts. A known starting state per class makes failures repeatable. Ownership is also the most expensive bug a multi-user app can ship (broken object level authorization is first on the OWASP API list), so it deserves a test for every verb. Today's React part tests the other risky corner: the refresh wrapper.

### What you'll build
- A `ResetAsync()` on the database fixture that deletes rows in foreign key order: notes, interviews, applications, companies, refresh tokens, user roles, users
- Each test class implementing `IAsyncLifetime` and calling the reset in `InitializeAsync`
- A small arrange helper: `CreateApplicationAs(userId)` returning the new id

- `AdminTests`: anonymous 401, normal user 403, admin 200 on `/api/admin/stats`

1. List your tables and their foreign keys. Write the delete order once, in one place.
2. Use `ExecuteDeleteAsync()` per table, or plain SQL. A library such as Respawn is fine too.
3. Call the reset at the start of each class, not the end, so a crashed run cannot poison the next.

- [ ] The suite passes in any order

- `EnsureDeleted` and migrate per class, which is slow.

### Why this matters
Week 8's shared refresh is subtle: if two 401s each start a refresh, the second presents a token that was already rotated, reuse detection revokes the family, and the user is logged out. Clicking around cannot prove this works. A network-level test can, and it guards the most fragile code in your client. Today's .NET part tests ownership; this tests the session.

### What you'll build
- `src/lib/api.test.ts`
- A per-test counter for refresh calls, reset in `beforeEach`
- Handlers set with `server.use(...)`:
  - `GET /api/applications` and `GET /api/auth/me` return 401 for the old token and 200 for the new one
  - `POST /api/auth/refresh` increments the counter and returns a new token
- Tests: two parallel requests cause one refresh; a failed refresh calls the unauthorized handler once and rejects with the original `ApiError`

### Step by step
1. Read how `api.ts` stores the token and exposes `refreshAccessToken()`. Set an "old" token through the same path the app uses.
2. In handlers, read the `Authorization` header from `request.headers`.
3. Fire both calls with `Promise.all` and await them.
4. Assert the counter is 1 and both results hold data.
5. Second test: make refresh return 401, register a `vi.fn()` as the unauthorized handler, assert it ran once.
6. Break the wrapper on purpose (drop the shared promise) and watch the first test fail.

```ts
let refreshCalls = 0;
beforeEach(() => { refreshCalls = 0; });
// TODO: server.use(...) with the three handlers
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Exactly one refresh for two concurrent 401s
- [ ] Each original request is retried once, not in a loop
- [ ] The failure path is covered
- [ ] Module state (token, shared promise) is reset between tests

### Hints
- If `api.ts` keeps state in module variables, export a small reset function for tests, or use `vi.resetModules()` with a dynamic import.
- Count requests per endpoint too, to prove each was called twice (401, then 200).

### Common mistakes
- Testing with requests in sequence, which never exercises the race.
- Leaking the new token into the next test.

### Check your understanding
- Why would two refreshes log the user out?
- What makes the second 401 wait for the first refresh?
- Why test this at the network level?

### Why this matters
A dashboard is where people decide whether your app is useful. The naive way loads every row and counts in C#, which is fine for 20 rows and terrible for 20,000. A `GroupBy` that EF translates to SQL `GROUP BY` lets the database do the counting and send back four rows. Aggregates come up in every backend interview. Today's React part draws these numbers.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `feature/dashboard`:
- `StatsDto(Total, ByStatus, ResponseRate)` in Application, with `ByStatus` holding all four statuses
- `IStatsQueries.GetAsync(ct)` in Application and `StatsQueries` in Infrastructure, scoped to the current user and hiding soft-deleted rows (the global filter does that)
- `GET /api/stats` in its own route group with `RequireAuthorization()`
- An integration test (week 11): an empty user gets zeros, a seeded user gets the expected counts

### Step by step
1. Define the response rate in writing first, for example "share of applications no longer in `Applied`". Metrics need definitions.
2. Write the grouped query and read its SQL with `ToQueryString()` or the log.
3. Fill missing statuses with zero in C#, after the query: a status with no rows has no group.
4. Decide the rate for a user with zero applications, and handle it.
5. Map the endpoint and write the two tests.

```csharp
var byStatus = await apps
    .GroupBy(a => a.Status)
    .Select(g => new { Status = g.Key, Count = g.Count() })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

- [ ] Counting happens in SQL, not in memory
- [ ] All four statuses are present, zeros included
- [ ] Another user's data never counts
- [ ] A new user gets a rate without dividing by zero

### Hints
- If EF cannot translate a `GroupBy`, it throws rather than silently loading everything. Simplify the key or the projection.
- `Total` is the sum of the grouped counts; no second query needed.

### Common mistakes
- `ToListAsync()` before `GroupBy`, which groups in memory.
- Returning a dictionary keyed by enum numbers instead of status names.

### Check your understanding
- How do you know the grouping ran in SQL?
- Why are missing statuses filled in C# and not SQL?
- What is your response rate, exactly?

### Why this matters
"How am I doing over time?" needs a time series, and time series need careful definitions: which day starts a week, what time zone, what happens to an empty week. - `WeeklyActivity` added to `StatsDto`: a list of `(WeekStart, ApplicationsSent, InterviewsScheduled)`

5. Do the same for interviews, then read both SQL statements in the log.

```csharp
static DateOnly WeekStart(DateOnly d) =>
```

### Why this matters
N+1 is the most common ORM performance bug: one query for a list, then one more for every row. It is invisible with five rows in development and painful with fifty in production. "What is N+1 and how do you fix it?" is asked in almost every backend interview. You will create one on purpose, see it in the log, and remove it. Today's React part hunts the front-end equivalent: wasted renders.

### What you'll build
- Two new list fields on `ApplicationDto`: `NextInterviewAt?` and `NoteCount`, shown on the card
- First the naive version, on purpose: after loading a page, call the week 9 interview and note queries once per application
- Then the fix: both values computed inside the list projection as subqueries
- Query counts before and after, in your PR notes

### Step by step
1. Turn on SQL logging in Development if it is off.
2. Build the naive loop and load one page of 20. Count the queries: 1 + 2N.
3. Rewrite as one projection: `NextInterviewAt` as the minimum future `ScheduledAt`, `NoteCount` as `a.Notes.Count()`.
4. Read the new SQL: one statement with correlated subqueries.
5. Load the page again and count.
6. Add `NextInterviewAt` to the card in the web app (a small line, "Next: Tue 14:30").

```csharp
.Select(a => new ApplicationDto(
    // ...
    a.Interviews.Where(i => i.ScheduledAt > now).Min(i => (DateTimeOffset?)i.ScheduledAt),
    a.Notes.Count()))
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One SQL statement per page load for the list
- [ ] No lazy loading anywhere
- [ ] The list query still projects, no `Include`
- [ ] Counts written down before and after

### Hints
- Lazy loading proxies make N+1 invisible in code. This course never enabled them; know why.
- The nullable cast in `Min` keeps "no interviews" from throwing.

### Common mistakes
- Fixing N+1 with `Include`, loading every interview and note row just to count them.
- Counting in C# after loading the collections.

### Check your understanding
- How do you spot N+1 without a profiler?
- Why is a projection better than `Include` here?
- When might two queries beat one?

### Why this matters
`memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` are the most misused hooks in React. They only help when something expensive re-renders with props that did not really change, and only if every prop keeps the same identity. Used blindly they add noise and memory for nothing. ### Why this matters
Loading an application with two collections in one query multiplies rows: 10 interviews times 30 notes is 300 rows for one application, the cartesian explosion. A split query sends one query per collection instead, at the cost of more round trips and no single snapshot. Compiled queries skip EF's query translation on hot paths. Knowing these trade-offs, and measuring them, is senior-level EF. This closes the .NET side of the PR "Dashboard".

### What you'll build
- A test application seeded with about 10 interviews and 30 notes
- The detail read loaded both ways: one query with two collections, and the same with `AsSplitQuery()`
- For each: the SQL statements, rows returned and elapsed time, in the PR notes
- The version you keep, with one sentence on why
- Optional: the detail lookup as a compiled query with `EF.CompileAsyncQuery`, timed against the normal one

### Step by step
1. If your detail endpoint projects, build a temporary `Include` version for the comparison (week 9 did a smaller one).
2. Run the single query and count the rows SQL Server returns.
3. Add `AsSplitQuery()` and read the separate statements.
4. Time both with a `Stopwatch` over 50 runs after a warm-up.
5. Decide: projection, single or split. Write the reason.
6. Push and open the PR "Dashboard"; merge after today's React part.

```csharp
var app = await db.Applications
    .Include(a => a.Interviews).Include(a => a.Notes)
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .SingleOrDefaultAsync(a => a.Id == id, ct);
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both versions measured on the same data
- [ ] The row counts explain the difference
- [ ] The kept version is justified in writing
- [ ] Temporary code is removed

### Hints
- Split queries need a stable ordering to be consistent; EF warns when it cannot guarantee one.
- Compiled queries save translation time, usually microseconds. Use them only where the numbers say so.

### Common mistakes
- Making split queries the global default without measuring.
- Timing a single cold run.

### Check your understanding
- What is a cartesian explosion?
- What does a split query give up?
- When is a compiled query worth it?

Output caching stores whole responses; sometimes you want to cache data that several endpoints use. ### Why this matters
Debouncing reduces requests, but a slow response for "ac" can still arrive after the response for "acme" and overwrite it: a race condition. Cancelling the old request stops wasted work and wrong results. `AbortController` is the browser's standard way to cancel fetches, and TanStack Query passes one to every query for you. This uses the endpoint from today's .NET part and yesterday's debounced term.

### What you'll build
- A quick experiment first: a plain `useEffect` that fetches with an `AbortController` and aborts in cleanup, to see the mechanics
- Then the real version: `useCompanySearch(term)` with `useQuery`, key `companyKeys.search(debouncedTerm)`, the query's `signal` passed to `api.ts`, `enabled` only for two or more characters, and `placeholderData` keeping the previous results
- A suggestions list under the input (keyboard support can stay simple: a list of buttons)
- An MSW test with a short delay in the handler

### Step by step
1. Throttle the network to Slow 3G for the experiment.
2. Write the effect version, type fast, and watch requests turn "cancelled".
3. Ignore the `AbortError` on cancel: it is not a real error.
4. Replace it with `useQuery`. Check that `api.ts` forwards the signal to `fetch`.
5. Use `keepPreviousData` as `placeholderData` so the list does not flash empty between terms.
6. Write the test: type fast with `user-event`, assert the handler ran once.

```ts
export function useCompanySearch(term: string) {
  const debounced = useDebounce(term, 250);
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: companyKeys.search(debounced),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => searchCompanies(debounced, signal),
    // TODO: enabled, placeholderData
  });
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Old requests are cancelled, not just ignored
- [ ] No error appears for a cancelled request
- [ ] Searching under two characters sends nothing
- [ ] Results never flash empty while typing

### Hints

### Why this matters
SignalR does not store messages: anything sent while a tab is disconnected is simply gone. The client cannot fix what it cannot detect. If every event carries an id and a sequence number, a client that sees 7 after 5 knows it missed one and can refetch. Ids also let it ignore a duplicate. - `EventEnvelope<T>(Guid Id, string Epoch, long Seq, DateTimeOffset OccurredAt, T Payload)`

### Why this matters
Retries hide brief blips; timeouts stop one slow service from tying up your threads; a circuit breaker stops hammering a service that is down and fails fast instead. Each solves a different problem, and combined wrongly they make things worse. "Retry vs circuit breaker" is a classic interview question. Today's React part shows the user something useful while this fails.

### What you'll build
- `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` in Infrastructure
- `.AddStandardResilienceHandler(...)` on the company info client
- Options tuned and written down: attempt timeout about 2 s, total timeout about 6 s, 3 retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breaker sampling and break duration
- The endpoint mapping "circuit open" and "timeout" exceptions to 503 with `Retry-After`

### Step by step
1. Read the standard pipeline's order: rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker, attempt timeout. Draw it as nested boxes.
2. Add the handler with defaults and set the stub's fail rate to 0.5. Count attempts in the log.
3. Tune the options. The breaker's sampling duration must be at least twice the attempt timeout, or start-up validation fails.
4. Stop the stub, call until the circuit opens, then time a call.
5. Start the stub, wait the break duration, and watch the half-open probe close the circuit.
6. Set a 5 second delay and confirm the attempt timeout cuts it.

```csharp
.AddStandardResilienceHandler(o =>
{
    o.AttemptTimeout.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2);
    // TODO: total timeout, retries, circuit breaker
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Brief failures are retried, with jitter
- [ ] An open circuit fails fast
- [ ] No call waits longer than the total timeout
- [ ] Every option value has a written reason

### Hints
- Retrying a POST can run it twice on the server; retries need idempotent operations.
- Breaker state lives in memory, per client and per instance.

### Common mistakes
- Retrying on the client too, so retries multiply.
- An attempt timeout longer than the total timeout.

### Check your understanding
- Retry vs circuit breaker, with JobHunt examples?
- Why does jitter matter?
- What does half-open mean?

### Why this matters
The outbox holds events safely; now something must deliver them. A background publisher reads unprocessed rows and sends them to RabbitMQ, marking each only after the broker confirms it. If the broker is down, rows wait and go out later. Exchanges, queues and acknowledgements are the vocabulary of every message broker interview. ### What you'll build

### Why this matters
If an XSS bug ever slips through, a Content Security Policy is the second wall: the browser refuses to run scripts from anywhere you did not allow. A strict policy (no inline scripts, only your own origin) blocks most real attacks. Writing one and fixing what it breaks is a skill many front-end developers never practise. Today's .NET part secures the API's headers; this secures the page's.

### What you'll build
- A policy in one file (for example `web/csp.ts` or a text file): `default-src 'self'`, `script-src 'self'`, `connect-src 'self'` (covers `/api` and the `/hubs` WebSocket in modern browsers), `img-src 'self' data:`, `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`
- `preview.headers` in `vite.config.ts` serving it, first as `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, then enforced
- `/api` and `/hubs` proxied in preview too, so the app works there
- Every violation fixed in code, never with `'unsafe-inline'`

### Step by step
1. Read the MDN guide; note which directives cover scripts, styles, fetch and WebSockets.
2. Add the report-only header to `preview` and run `vite build` then `vite preview`.
3. Use every page and read the console.
4. Fix violations: inline `style` attributes from libraries may need `style-src` care; inline scripts must go.
5. Switch to the enforced header and repeat.
6. Keep the policy text in one place; week 20's nginx serves the same text.

```ts
preview: {
  headers: { "Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only": csp },
  // TODO: proxy /api and /hubs
},
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The CSP is enforced, not report-only
- [ ] No `'unsafe-inline'` or `'unsafe-eval'` in `script-src`
- [ ] Zero violations across the main flows
- [ ] One source of truth for the policy

### Hints
- The dev server injects inline scripts for hot reload, which is why you test on the production build.
- `frame-ancestors` does not work in a `<meta>` tag; serve the policy as a header.

### Common mistakes
- Testing the CSP on the dev server and giving up.
- Adding `'unsafe-inline'` to make warnings go away.

### Check your understanding
- What does a CSP do if an XSS bug exists?
- Why test with `vite preview`?
- Why start with report-only?

### Why this matters
In production the API sits behind a proxy (week 20's nginx, a load balancer). Every request then comes from the proxy's IP, so week 13's per-IP rate limit puts all users in one bucket, and HTTPS looks like HTTP. Forwarded headers fix that, but trusting them from anyone lets an attacker pick their own IP and dodge every limit. Trusting only known proxies is the whole trick. Today's React part keeps tokens out of URLs.

### What you'll build
- `ForwardedHeadersOptions` with `XForwardedFor` and `XForwardedProto`
- Trusted proxies or networks read from configuration (`ForwardedHeaders:KnownProxies`), empty by default
- `UseForwardedHeaders()` first in the pipeline, before HTTPS redirection, authentication and rate limiting
- The rate limiter partition logging the client IP it used, at `Debug`
- The week 13 TODO comment removed, and a line in `SECURITY.md` about trusted proxies

### Step by step
1. Read the proxy page's section on forwarded headers and the default trust rules.
2. Configure the options; bind the known proxy list from configuration.
3. Move `UseForwardedHeaders()` to the top of the pipeline.
4. Log the partition key in the rate limiter.
5. With loopback trusted, send requests with a forwarded IP and watch the key change.
6. Remove loopback from the list and repeat: the header is ignored.

```csharp
builder.Services.Configure<ForwardedHeadersOptions>(o =>
{
    o.ForwardedHeaders = ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto;
    // TODO: known proxies or networks from configuration
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Forwarded headers are honoured only from trusted proxies
- [ ] The middleware runs first
- [ ] Rate limiting sees the real client IP behind a proxy
- [ ] The week 13 TODO is closed

### Hints
- Week 20 sets the trusted network to the Docker network nginx uses.
- `X-Forwarded-Proto` matters for HTTPS redirection and for `Secure` cookies behind a proxy.

### Common mistakes
- Clearing the known proxy lists so every sender is trusted.
- Placing the middleware after authentication or rate limiting.

### Check your understanding
- What breaks behind a proxy without forwarded headers?
- Why must the proxy list be restricted?
- Why does the middleware's position matter?

### Why this matters
Orchestrators and load balancers ask two questions: is the process alive (restart it if not), and is it ready for traffic (stop sending requests if not)? - `/health/live` with a predicate that runs no checks
- `/health/ready` running checks tagged `ready`, with a JSON response writer listing each check's status and duration
- Both anonymous, both without sensitive details

```csharp
{

});
```

Only an end-to-end test proves the layers work together in a real browser: cookies, refresh, routing, the board. Playwright's role-based locators and auto-waiting make these tests readable and stable. It uses the E2E environment from Wednesday's .NET part and the health check from today's.

### What you'll build
- `e2e/` at the repo root with its own `package.json`, created with `npm init playwright@latest`
- `playwright.config.ts`: `webServer` entries for the API (environment `E2E`, ready when `/health/ready` answers) and the web app, `baseURL`, Chromium and Firefox projects
- A global setup running Wednesday's reset command
- A `loggedInPage` fixture that registers a unique user through `page.request` (so the refresh cookie lands in that browser context), then opens the app
- `journey.spec.ts` using `getByRole` and `getByLabel` only

### Step by step
1. Plan each journey step with a role-based locator before writing code.
2. Set up the folder, config and two web servers. Reuse running servers locally, never in CI.
3. Write the global setup.
4. Write the fixture with a fresh email per test (`crypto.randomUUID()`).
5. Move the card with the week 10 keyboard controls; they are deterministic, unlike mouse drags.
6. Assert what users see with web-first assertions (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`).
7. Add a root `test:e2e` script.

```ts
export const test = base.extend<{ loggedInPage: Page }>({
  loggedInPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // TODO: register and log in via page.request, goto("/applications")
    await use(page);
  },
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The journey passes in two browsers
- [ ] Every test has its own user
- [ ] No CSS selectors or test ids
- [ ] One command runs everything

### Hints
- Sharing one saved `storageState` is the usual advice, but week 8's rotation would see the second use of the same refresh token as reuse and revoke the session. Logging in fresh per test avoids that; write it in `TESTING.md`.
- Test the register form once in the UI; fixtures can use the API.

### Common mistakes
- `page.waitForTimeout` instead of web-first assertions.
- Tests that depend on each other's data or order.

### Check your understanding
- Why does a shared session break with refresh token rotation?
- Why prefer role-based locators?
- Why move the card with the keyboard in tests?
19-4-api:
### Why this matters
A deploy that "succeeded" can still be broken: a missing secret, a failed migration, a bad connection string. A smoke test is a tiny, fast check run right after every deploy, hitting the few things that must work. If it fails, you roll back before users notice. Week 20's pipeline runs this script. This closes the .NET side of the PR "Polish + E2E".

### What you'll build
- `scripts/smoke.sh` (bash with `curl`) or `smoke.ps1`, or a Playwright API test in `/e2e`; pick one and write why
- Input: base URL argument; smoke user email and password from environment variables, never in the script
- Steps: `/health/ready` is 200; login returns a token; `GET /api/applications?pageSize=1` with it returns 200 and the expected JSON shape
- A clear line per step, and a non-zero exit code on the first failure
- A smoke user seeded in each environment (Tuesday's seeder can create it outside Production; production gets one created once by hand)
- The script documented in the README

### Step by step
1. Decide what "the app works" means in three checks.
2. Write the health step with a short retry loop: a fresh deploy may need seconds to become ready.
3. Write the login step and extract the token.
4. Write the read step and check one field of the response.
5. Run it against the local stack, then break it (wrong password, stopped database) and watch it fail.
6. Push and open the PR "Polish + E2E"; merge after today's React part.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Runs in under 30 seconds
- [ ] Fails loudly with a non-zero exit code
- [ ] No credentials in the script or repo
- [ ] Read-only: it never writes data

### Hints
- The rate limit on login (week 13) applies to the smoke test too; one login per run is fine.
- A smoke test is not an E2E suite: keep it to the critical path.

### Common mistakes
- Smoke tests that create data in production.
- Ignoring the exit code, so a failure looks like success in CI.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between a smoke test and an E2E test?
- Why read-only?
- What should happen when the smoke test fails after a deploy?
19-4-web:
### Why this matters
A test that fails one run in ten teaches the team to ignore red builds. Flakiness has causes: asserting before a refetch finished, a toast covering a button, shared data. Playwright traces record every action, DOM snapshot and network call, so you can see the cause instead of guessing. Retries hide flakes; finding them is the skill. It ends the week with the PR "Polish + E2E", together with today's .NET part.

### What you'll build
- `trace: "on-first-retry"`, screenshots on failure, `retries` of 2 in CI and 0 locally
- `realtime.spec.ts`: two pages in one browser context (like two tabs sharing the refresh cookie), move a card in one, assert it moves in the other (week 15)
- `--repeat-each=3` runs until green with no retries
- A flake log in the PR: symptom, trace evidence, cause, fix
- `TESTING.md` updated with the E2E layer

### Step by step
1. Run with `--repeat-each=3` and note any failure.
2. Open the trace with `npx playwright show-trace` and step through actions, snapshots, network and console.
3. Fix causes, not symptoms: wait for the specific response or use a web-first assertion; never a fixed sleep.
4. Write the realtime spec with `context.newPage()`.
5. Run three times in a row: all green, no retries.
6. Run all builds and tests, push, review and merge PR "Polish + E2E".

```ts
test("board updates in another tab", async ({ loggedInPage: a, context }) => {
  const b = await context.newPage();
  // TODO: open the board in both, move in a, expect the card in b's new column
});
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Three consecutive green runs with zero retries
- [ ] The realtime test passes
- [ ] Each flake has a written cause
- [ ] PR "Polish + E2E" is merged

### Hints
- Playwright marks tests that pass only on retry as flaky; treat that as a failure to investigate.
- Two pages in one context share cookies like tabs; two contexts are like two browsers.

### Common mistakes
- Raising timeouts until the flake disappears.
- Turning on retries locally and calling it fixed.

### Check your understanding
- What does a trace show that a screenshot does not?
- Why are retries dangerous as a fix?
- Why one context for the realtime test?

### Why this matters
"Works on my machine" ends when the machine is an image. A multi-stage build compiles with the full SDK and ships only the small runtime with your published output, so images are smaller and carry no compilers or source. Running as a non-root user limits what an attacker can do after a break-in. Writing a Dockerfile from memory is part of this week's checkpoint. Today's React part packages the web app the same way.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `feature/ship-it`:
- `api/Dockerfile` with stages: `build` (the .NET 10 SDK image), `publish`, and `final` (the ASP.NET Core 10 runtime image)
- Layer caching: copy the `.csproj` files and restore first, then copy the source
- `dotnet publish -c Release` into `/app`
- The final stage running as the non-root user the .NET images provide (`USER $APP_UID`), on port 8080
- A writable uploads folder owned by that user (until Thursday moves files to blob storage)
- `api/.dockerignore` excluding `bin`, `obj`, `.git`, `.env` and test output
- The `docker` ecosystem added to Dependabot (week 18)

### Step by step
1. Sketch the stages and what each copies.
2. Write build and publish. Build once, change one `.cs` file, build again: restore comes from cache.
3. Write the final stage: copy only the published output.
4. Set the user and port; confirm with `docker exec <id> whoami`.
5. Run it with settings as environment variables (`Jwt__SigningKey`, `ConnectionStrings__JobHunt`) pointing at your local SQL Server.
6. Record the image size in the PR.

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
# TODO: copy csproj files keeping folders, restore, copy source, publish to /app
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The final image has no SDK or source
- [ ] It runs as a non-root user
- [ ] All settings come from the environment
- [ ] Restore is cached between builds

### Hints
- `docker history <image>` shows each layer; a secret copied into any layer can leak.
- The .NET SDK can also build images without a Dockerfile; knowing the Dockerfile way makes that easy to read.

### Common mistakes
- `COPY . .` before restore, so every code change re-downloads packages.
- Baking `appsettings.Development.json` or secrets into the image.

### Check your understanding
- What does each stage contribute?
- Why restore before copying the source?
- Why run as non-root, and why port 8080?
20-0-web:
### Why this matters
In production there is no Vite dev server: the app is static files, and something must serve them. nginx is small and fast, but a SPA needs one special rule: any unknown path returns `index.html` so React Router can handle it, or every deep link 404s on reload. Caching rules decide whether users get new releases. Today's .NET part builds the API image; tomorrow nginx also proxies to it.

### What you'll build
- `web/Dockerfile`: a Node LTS stage running `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then an unprivileged nginx stage serving `dist`
- `web/nginx.conf` with:
  - `try_files $uri /index.html` for SPA routes
  - long `Cache-Control` with `immutable` for hashed `/assets/`, `no-cache` for `index.html`
  - the week 18 CSP and security headers with `add_header ... always`
- `web/.dockerignore` excluding `node_modules`, `dist` and `.env*`

### Step by step
1. Write the Dockerfile; `npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says.
2. Write a server block serving `dist` with the SPA fallback.
3. Add the cache rules: hashed files forever, the HTML entry never.
4. Paste the CSP text from week 18 into a header.
5. Build and run the image; open a deep link and reload.
6. Check headers in the Network tab.

```nginx
location / {
    try_files $uri /index.html;
}
# TODO: location /assets/ with long immutable caching
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deep links survive a reload
- [ ] Assets are cached, `index.html` is revalidated
- [ ] The CSP is a response header
- [ ] nginx runs unprivileged

### Hints
- `add_header` in a `location` replaces headers from the outer block; repeat them or use an include file.
- Unprivileged nginx images listen on 8080, like the API.

### Common mistakes
- Caching `index.html`, so users never get the new release.
- A fallback that also catches `/api`, returning HTML to API calls (tomorrow fixes routing).

### Check your understanding
- Why does a SPA need a fallback rule?
- Why cache assets forever but not `index.html`?
- What did the Vite dev server do that nginx must now do?

### Why this matters
JobHunt now depends on four services. A new developer (or a reviewer) should run one command, not follow ten setup steps. Compose describes the whole stack, and health checks make services wait for each other instead of crashing at start-up. Tomorrow's migrator and nginx plug into this file. Today's React part routes traffic to the API through nginx.

### What you'll build
- `compose.yaml` at the repo root with `sqlserver`, `redis`, `rabbitmq` (management image), `mailpit` (or your catcher) and `api`
- Health checks: `sqlcmd` for SQL Server, `redis-cli ping`, `rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping`, and the API's `/health/ready` (week 19)
- `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`
- Named volumes for SQL Server and RabbitMQ data
- Settings from `.env` (week 18's `.env.example`), never in `compose.yaml`; services reached by name (`sqlserver`, `redis`), not `localhost`
- Only tool UIs publishing ports for now; tomorrow `web` becomes the single entry point

### Step by step
1. Write the infrastructure services and get each healthy with `docker compose ps`.
2. Add the API with `build: ./api` and its environment.
3. Add `depends_on` conditions.
4. Apply migrations by hand once for today; Wednesday adds the migrator.
5. Read `docker compose logs -f api` until start-up is clean.
6. Run `down -v` and `up` again from scratch.

```yaml
api:
  build: ./api
  env_file: .env
  depends_on:
    sqlserver: { condition: service_healthy }
    # TODO: redis, rabbitmq
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One command starts the stack
- [ ] Services wait for healthy dependencies
- [ ] No secrets in `compose.yaml`
- [ ] Data survives `down` without `-v`

### Hints
- SQL Server takes a while to start; give its health check a start period.
- Week 18's trusted proxy list will need the Compose network range tomorrow.

### Common mistakes
- `localhost` in connection strings inside containers.
- `depends_on` without a condition, which only orders start, not readiness.

### Check your understanding
- Why health checks and not just start order?
- How do services find each other?
- What does `-v` delete?

### Why this matters
Since week 3 the Vite proxy has quietly made everything same-origin: cookies just worked, CORS was not needed, and week 15's WebSocket went through untouched. In production nginx takes that job. Missing one piece (the WebSocket upgrade headers, the body size limit, forwarded headers) breaks a feature only in production. This puts today's .NET Compose stack behind one entry point.

### What you'll build
- `location /api/` and `location /hubs/` in `nginx.conf` proxying to `http://api:8080`
- For `/hubs`: HTTP/1.1 and the `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers, plus a longer read timeout
- `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` set on both locations
- `client_max_body_size` slightly above week 14's 5 MB limit
- The API's trusted proxy list (week 18) set to the Compose network, so forwarded headers from nginx are honoured and nobody else's are
- `web` added to `compose.yaml` as the only service publishing a port
- `/hangfire` not routed (Friday decides how admins reach it)

### Step by step
1. List everything the Vite proxy did in weeks 3, 8, 14 and 15; each needs an nginx line or a decision.
2. Add the two locations before the SPA fallback, so API calls never get `index.html`.
3. Add the WebSocket headers and check the Network tab shows status 101 for `/hubs`.
4. Add forwarded headers and set the API's trusted network.
5. Log in, reload (refresh cookie), open two tabs (live updates), upload a file.
6. Check a rate-limited login logs the real client IP, not nginx's.

```nginx
location /hubs/ {
    proxy_pass http://api:8080;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    # TODO: Upgrade and Connection headers, forwarded headers, read timeout
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every feature works through nginx alone
- [ ] `/hubs` uses a WebSocket, not long polling
- [ ] Uploads up to the limit pass
- [ ] Forwarded headers are trusted only from nginx

### Hints
- Same origin through nginx means the refresh cookie and CORS need no changes.
- If live updates fall back to long polling, the upgrade headers are missing.

### Common mistakes
- Putting the SPA fallback first, so `/api` returns HTML.
- Forgetting the body size, so uploads fail with 413 only in production.

### Check your understanding
- What did the Vite proxy do that you now configure?
- Why do WebSockets need special headers?
- Why must the API trust only nginx's forwarded headers?

### Why this matters
Calling `Migrate()` at start-up seems easy, until two instances start together and race, or a migration fails halfway through a deploy. A migrations bundle is a single executable that applies pending migrations as a separate step before the new version starts. Expand and contract keeps old and new versions working during the switch. Both are standard answers to "how do you deploy schema changes?". Today's React part makes one web image fit every environment.

### What you'll build
- A `migrator` stage in `api/Dockerfile` running `dotnet ef migrations bundle` into a single executable
- A `migrator` service in `compose.yaml`: built with `target: migrator`, connection string from `.env`, runs once and exits
- The API's `depends_on` waiting for `service_completed_successfully`
- Any start-up `Migrate()` call removed (week 19's E2E reset keeps its own explicit path)
- A note in the PR describing expand and contract with a JobHunt example

### Step by step
1. Read the applying migrations page, sections on bundles and on applying at runtime.
2. Add the stage; the bundle needs the EF tools, so build it in an SDK-based stage.
3. Run the bundle once by hand against your local SQL Server with `--connection`.
4. Add the Compose service and the API's dependency.
5. `down -v`, `up`: the migrator runs, exits 0, then the API starts.
6. Write the expand and contract example: renaming a column as add new, copy, switch code, drop old across releases.

```yaml
migrator:
  build: { context: ./api, target: migrator }
  depends_on:
    sqlserver: { condition: service_healthy }
  # TODO: connection string from .env
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Migrations run as a separate step
- [ ] A failed migration stops the API from starting
- [ ] No start-up `Migrate()` in production code
- [ ] Expand and contract is explained with an example

### Hints
- Friday's pipeline runs the same bundle before rolling out a new revision.
- A bundle is idempotent: it applies only pending migrations.

### Common mistakes
- Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
- Running migrations from every API instance at start-up.

### Check your understanding
- Why a separate step instead of start-up migration?
- What does expand and contract protect against?
- What happens if the migrator fails?

### Why this matters
One instance can keep state in memory; two cannot. With two API instances, a SignalR message sent on instance A never reaches a tab connected to B, an output cache eviction clears only one copy, a cookie protected with A's keys fails on B, and a file saved on A's disk is missing on B. - Data Protection keys persisted to Redis or blob storage with one application name, so the week 14 dashboard cookie works anywhere
- `BlobFileStorage : IFileStorage` with `Azure.Storage.Blobs`, chosen by configuration, and Azurite in Compose
- Notes on what stays per instance: rate limit counters (week 13), the event sequencer (week 15, the epoch makes clients resync), the outbox publisher (week 17: needs locked-row skipping or a lease)

5. Scale to two and test each fix with two tabs.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every row in `SCALING.md` has a fix or an accepted limit
- [ ] Live updates cross instances
- [ ] Cookies and cache eviction work on either instance
- [ ] Files are shared storage, not local disk

### Hints
- With several instances, SignalR needs sticky sessions unless clients use WebSockets only and skip negotiation; note your choice.
- Hangfire with SQL Server storage already coordinates several servers.

### Why this matters
CI that can be skipped is a suggestion. Required checks make "green before merge" a rule, and coverage thresholds stop the slow slide where each pull request adds untested code. This lesson lives in the React lane but covers both apps' gates, since they protect one repository together. It ends the week with the PR "Ship it", together with today's .NET part.

### What you'll build
- An `api` job in `ci.yml`: `actions/setup-dotnet` for .NET 10, NuGet caching, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test` with coverage (Docker is available on Ubuntu runners, so Testcontainers works)
- A .NET coverage threshold that fails the job when merged line coverage drops, using week 11's report or the coverage collector's threshold option
- Vitest `coverage.thresholds` set a little below today's numbers (the week 11 stretch, now enforced)
- Optional: the week 19 E2E job needing both, uploading traces on failure
- A ruleset on main: pull request required, `web` and `api` checks required, no force pushes
- PR "Ship it" merged through the rules

### Step by step
1. Add the `api` job next to Thursday's `web` job; they run in parallel.
2. Exclude migrations from coverage as in week 11.
3. Add the .NET threshold and check it fails when you lower the number on purpose.
4. Add Vitest thresholds the same way.
5. Create the ruleset in the repository settings and select both checks.
6. Run all builds and tests, push, review and merge PR "Ship it" through the ruleset.

```yaml
api:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  defaults: { run: { working-directory: api } }
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    # TODO: setup-dotnet, restore with cache, test with coverage, threshold
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both jobs run on every pull request
- [ ] Each fails below its coverage threshold
- [ ] main cannot be changed without green checks
- [ ] PR "Ship it" is merged

### Hints
- Set thresholds slightly below today's numbers so they stop regressions without blocking you.
- Upload coverage reports as artifacts so reviewers can see what changed.

### Common mistakes
- Thresholds at 100%, so people write empty tests.
- Required checks with names that do not match the job names.

### Check your understanding
- What does a required check guarantee?
- Why thresholds below current coverage?
- Why run the API and web jobs in parallel?

### Why this matters
After 20 weeks, JobHunt has more moving parts than most take-home projects: cache, queues, jobs, real-time. A reviewer needs a map before reading code, and an interviewer will ask "why did you choose X?". C4 diagrams give the map at the right zoom level; ADRs record each decision with the alternatives you rejected. Today's React part documents the front end the same way.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `release/v1.0`:
- `docs/architecture.md` with two Mermaid diagrams:
  - level 1, context: the user, JobHunt, email, the company info service
  - level 2, containers: browser SPA, nginx, API (with Hangfire inside), SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, blob storage, SMTP, the trace collector
- Arrows labelled with protocol and purpose ("HTTPS JSON", "WebSocket push", "AMQP events")
- `docs/adr/0001-...md` onward for the API side, for example:
  - refresh tokens hashed in an httpOnly cookie, access token in memory (week 8)
  - rowversion optimistic concurrency with 409 (week 10)
  - Hangfire instead of hosted services (week 14)
  - outbox plus RabbitMQ instead of publishing in the request (week 17)
- A template in `docs/adr/README.md`

### Step by step
1. List the ten biggest API decisions; circle four.
2. Draw level 1 on paper: JobHunt as one box, everything else around it.
3. Draw level 2: every container you deploy or depend on, and how they talk.
4. Write both in Mermaid and check they render in a GitHub preview.
5. Write each ADR in under a page: context, decision, alternatives, consequences (good and bad), status.
6. Add the obvious challenge to each ADR and your answer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  user([Job seeker]) -->|HTTPS| web[SPA via nginx]
  web -->|/api JSON, /hubs WebSocket| api[JobHunt API]
  %% TODO: SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, blob, SMTP
```

- [ ] Both diagrams render on GitHub
- [ ] Every arrow is labelled
- [ ] Each ADR names rejected alternatives
- [ ] Consequences include a downside

### Hints

- ADRs are immutable: a changed mind is a new ADR that supersedes the old one.

### Common mistakes

### Check your understanding
- What does each C4 level show, and for whom?
- What makes an ADR useful years later?

Front-end architecture is often undocumented, so every new developer rediscovers where data lives and why. ### Why this matters
"Is it fast?" needs a number and a target. Averages hide the slow requests users remember; the 95th percentile shows them. A latency budget written before measuring keeps you honest, and a small load test finds problems one request never shows: lock contention, connection pool limits, cache stampedes. Today's React part does the same with Lighthouse.

### What you'll build
- Budgets in `PERFORMANCE.md`: p95 under 200 ms for list and detail, under 100 ms for cached stats, under 300 ms for a status change
- The demo seeder (week 19) plus extra rows so the database is realistic
- A small load: a few concurrent users for a minute, with a tool of your choice or a short script firing concurrent requests
- p95 read from the built-in `http.server.request.duration` metric (week 13's `dotnet-counters` works) or from your traces (week 16)
- The worst endpoint fixed and measured again the same way

### Step by step
1. Write the budgets first, so you cannot move the goalposts.
2. Run the compose stack (week 20) in Release, not the debugger.
3. Run the load and collect p95 per endpoint.
4. Open a trace of the slowest endpoint and find the slowest span.
5. Fix it with week 12 habits: an index, a projection, a cache, less work.
6. Measure again and record both numbers.

```md
| Endpoint            | Budget p95 | Before | After |
| ------------------- | ---------- | ------ | ----- |
| GET /api/applications | 200 ms   |        |       |
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Budgets written before measuring
- [ ] p95, not averages
- [ ] One fix with before and after
- [ ] Measured on the production build

### Hints
- Warm up before measuring; the first requests pay for JIT and connection pools.
- Rate limits (week 13) can throttle your own load test; raise them for the run.

### Common mistakes
- Measuring in Debug with the debugger attached.
- Changing two things between runs.

### Check your understanding
- Why p95 instead of the average?
- What can a load test find that one request cannot?
- What was the worst endpoint and why?
